distros.name: Linux Mint (Cinnamon)

highlights.beginner: The most common first Linux: everything is point-and-click, with a friendly Welcome screen.
highlights.windows_like: Looks and works like Windows: taskbar, start menu and system tray in the usual places.
highlights.nvidia: The Driver Manager installs NVIDIA's driver with one click.
highlights.stable: Based on Ubuntu LTS, so updates are calm and well tested.
highlights.community: Huge community; almost any question already has an answer online.
highlights.privacy: No telemetry, and no Snap store forced on you.
highlights.out_of_box: Media codecs and the driver manager are offered right in the installer.

caveats: Software versions lag behind Fedora and Arch-based distros by several months.

distros.name: Ubuntu Desktop

highlights.community: The most widely used desktop Linux: most software and guides target it first.
highlights.nvidia: 'Additional Drivers' installs NVIDIA's driver with a checkbox.
highlights.stable: Long-term-support releases get five years of updates.
highlights.dev: The default target for most developer tools, Docker guides and CUDA.
highlights.creative: Commercial creative apps that ship Linux versions usually test on Ubuntu first.
highlights.enterprise: The Linux most companies, clouds and universities standardise on.
highlights.software_range: Almost every Linux app publishes an Ubuntu package first.

caveats: Pushes Snap packages (slower to start, Canonical-controlled store).
Sends optional system info to Canonical unless you opt out.

distros.name: Kubuntu

highlights.windows_like: KDE Plasma's layout feels very close to Windows 10/11.
highlights.customizable: Plasma can be customised more than any other desktop, without the terminal.
highlights.community: Ubuntu underneath, so Ubuntu guides and software apply.
highlights.nvidia: Driver Manager installs NVIDIA's driver with a few clicks.

caveats: Plasma versions lag behind Fedora KDE and openSUSE.
Also uses Snap packages by default.

distros.name: Fedora Workstation

highlights.fresh: Recent software and kernels every six months, without being an experiment.
highlights.modern_look: A clean, modern GNOME desktop as its designers intended (closer to macOS than Windows).
highlights.dev: A favourite of developers: up-to-date compilers, toolbox containers and Podman built in.
highlights.privacy: Community-run project with no ads or tracking.
highlights.foss: Ships only free software by default; Red Hat's upstream, so skills transfer to work.
highlights.rhel_family: Fedora is where Red Hat Enterprise Linux comes from, so the tools match what Red Hat shops use.

caveats: NVIDIA's driver needs the RPM Fusion repository enabled first (a few steps).
Some media codecs need an extra repository.
A new release every six months: plan a short upgrade about twice a year.

distros.name: Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop

highlights.windows_like: A Windows-style taskbar and start menu with the latest KDE Plasma.
highlights.fresh: Recent Plasma, kernels and drivers every six months.
highlights.customizable: Plasma lets you change almost everything without the terminal.
highlights.dev: Same developer-friendly base as Fedora Workstation.

caveats: NVIDIA's driver needs the RPM Fusion repository enabled first (a few steps).
A new release every six months: plan a short upgrade about twice a year.

distros.name: Pop!_OS

highlights.nvidia: Has a separate download with NVIDIA's driver already installed: no setup at all.
highlights.dev: Made by a PC maker for developers: CUDA and dev tooling are easy.
highlights.creative: Aimed at creators too: with the NVIDIA download, GPU apps like Blender and DaVinci Resolve have their driver ready.
highlights.gaming: Steam and GPU drivers work out of the box.
highlights.beginner: Friendly setup and a keyboard-driven tiling option when you want it.
highlights.out_of_box: Codecs, drivers and Flatpak are set up for you.

caveats: Historically needs Secure Boot turned off to install; check the current release notes.
Its new COSMIC desktop is young, so expect some rough edges.

distros.name: Bazzite

highlights.gaming: Built for gaming: Steam, Proton tweaks, controller support and HDR preinstalled.
highlights.nvidia: Has a ready-made NVIDIA edition, so the driver is already there.
highlights.low_maintenance: Updates apply as a whole image and can be rolled back from the boot menu if anything breaks.
highlights.stable: The core system is read-only, so it is very hard to break by accident.

caveats: The read-only core makes classic 'install any package' tinkering harder; apps come from Flatpak or containers.
With Secure Boot on, you enrol a key once during install.
Wants a reasonably modern PC (8 GB+ RAM).

distros.name: Debian
distros.desktop: GNOME by default (KDE, Xfce, Cinnamon offered)

highlights.stable: Famously rock-solid: a release changes very little for about two years.
highlights.privacy: A volunteer, non-commercial project with a strong free-software and privacy stance.
highlights.light: Runs well on older machines, especially with the Xfce desktop.
highlights.software_range: One of the largest software collections of any distro (tens of thousands of packages).
highlights.foss: Free software by default, with non-free firmware clearly separated.

caveats: Software is often a year or more old.
NVIDIA drivers and some setup steps are manual.
The installer asks more technical questions than Mint or Ubuntu.

distros.name: openSUSE Tumbleweed

highlights.fresh: Rolling release: you always have the latest software, with no big version upgrades.
highlights.stable: The most tested rolling release: every update passes automated openQA testing, and snapshots let you roll back from the boot menu.
highlights.customizable: YaST gives a graphical control panel for almost every system setting.

caveats: Updates are frequent and large, so you should update weekly.
Smaller English-speaking community than Ubuntu or Fedora.

distros.name: Zorin OS Core

highlights.windows_like: Designed specifically for people leaving Windows; you can pick a Windows-style layout.
highlights.beginner: Polished and simple, with Windows app support set up for you.
highlights.modern_look: One of the most polished-looking desktops out of the box.

caveats: Releases follow Ubuntu LTS but often arrive months later.
Some layouts and extras are in the paid Pro edition.

distros.name: MX Linux (Xfce)

highlights.light: Very light: makes old or low-memory PCs feel quick again.
highlights.stable: Built on Debian stable, so very little changes under you.
highlights.beginner: The 'MX Tools' collection puts common admin jobs in simple windows.

caveats: Looks dated compared with GNOME or KDE.
Not ideal for gaming or the newest hardware.

distros.name: Linux Mint (Xfce)

highlights.light: Mint's lightest edition: the same friendly tools on older hardware.
highlights.beginner: Same Welcome screen, Driver Manager and update tool as Mint Cinnamon.

caveats: Looks plainer than the Cinnamon edition.

distros.name: Xubuntu

highlights.light: Ubuntu with the light Xfce desktop: good on older PCs.
highlights.software_range: All of Ubuntu's software and guides apply.

caveats: Uses Snap packages like Ubuntu.

distros.name: Lubuntu

highlights.light: One of the lightest Ubuntu flavours (LXQt desktop).
highlights.software_range: All of Ubuntu's software and guides apply.

caveats: Fewer graphical settings tools than the bigger desktops.

distros.name: Ubuntu MATE

highlights.light: A traditional, lightweight desktop that stays out of your way.
highlights.customizable: MATE Tweak switches between Windows-, Mac- and classic layouts in one click.

caveats: Smaller team than Ubuntu's main edition.

distros.name: elementary OS

highlights.beginner: Very simple: few settings to get lost in.
highlights.privacy: Funded by its users; no tracking or ads.

caveats: Deliberately limited customisation.
Releases trail Ubuntu LTS by months.

distros.name: Fedora Silverblue

highlights.stable: Read-only core with whole-system updates you can roll back from the boot menu.
highlights.low_maintenance: Updates install in the background and apply on next boot.
highlights.dev: Built around Toolbox containers for development.

caveats: Apps come mainly from Flatpak; installing system packages is a different workflow.
NVIDIA drivers need extra steps (Bazzite is the easier atomic option for NVIDIA).

distros.name: Nobara

highlights.gaming: Fedora tuned for gaming and streaming by the maintainer of Proton-GE.
highlights.nvidia: NVIDIA drivers, codecs and OBS are set up for you.

caveats: Run by a very small team; fixes depend on a few people.
Fast-moving, so occasional breakage is more likely than on Mint or Ubuntu.

distros.name: antiX

highlights.light: Extremely light: runs on very old PCs with 1 GB of RAM or less.
highlights.privacy: No systemd, no telemetry, very minimal.

caveats: Very spartan look and tools.
Not suitable for gaming or modern GPUs.

distros.name: Linux Lite

highlights.beginner: Aimed squarely at Windows users on older PCs, with clear help manuals.
highlights.light: Light Xfce desktop on an Ubuntu LTS base.

caveats: Small team; releases follow Ubuntu LTS.

distros.name: Arch Linux

highlights.diy: You build the system yourself, so you learn exactly how it works.
highlights.software_range: Official repos plus the AUR: nearly every Linux program exists here.
highlights.fresh: Rolling release with the latest everything.
highlights.community: The Arch Wiki is the best Linux documentation there is.

caveats: Installation is manual (archinstall helps, but it is still technical).
Install media doesn't boot with Secure Boot on; it can be set up afterwards.
You are responsible for reading news before updates.

distros.name: EndeavourOS

highlights.fresh: Arch with a graphical installer: rolling and up to date.
highlights.software_range: Full access to Arch's repos and the AUR.
highlights.community: Known for a friendly forum, plus the Arch Wiki.

caveats: Still Arch underneath: expect to use the terminal for maintenance.
Needs Secure Boot turned off to install.

distros.name: Manjaro

highlights.beginner: A friendlier, graphical way into the Arch world.
highlights.nvidia: Hardware tool installs NVIDIA drivers automatically.
highlights.software_range: Its own repos plus (with care) the AUR.

caveats: Its delayed repos can clash with AUR packages built for current Arch.
Has a history of project-management slip-ups (e.g. expired website certificates).

distros.name: CachyOS

highlights.gaming: Performance-tuned kernels and packages, with a gaming setup option.
highlights.nvidia: Detects your GPU and installs the right driver during setup.

caveats: Arch-based: occasional manual fixes after updates.
Younger, smaller project than Fedora or Ubuntu.
Needs Secure Boot turned off to install.

distros.name: Garuda Linux

highlights.out_of_box: Gaming tools, codecs and drivers come preinstalled.
highlights.stable: Automatic Btrfs snapshots before updates let you roll back.
highlights.modern_look: Flashy, heavily themed desktop out of the box.

caveats: Heavy: wants a fairly modern PC.
Arch-based rolling release.
Needs Secure Boot turned off to install.

distros.name: openSUSE Leap

highlights.stable: Shares its core with SUSE Linux Enterprise: built for long, calm releases.
highlights.enterprise: Close match to SUSE's enterprise Linux.
highlights.customizable: YaST gives a graphical control panel for almost every system setting.

caveats: Software and drivers are older than Tumbleweed or Fedora.
Some codecs need the community Packman repository.

distros.name: NixOS

highlights.diy: The whole system is described in one config file: rebuild it anywhere, identically.
highlights.stable: Every change is a new 'generation' you can roll back to from the boot menu.
highlights.software_range: Nixpkgs is one of the largest package collections of any distro.

caveats: Steep learning curve: it works very differently from other Linux distros.
Many normal Linux how-to guides don't apply directly.
Needs Secure Boot turned off to install.

distros.name: Void Linux
distros.desktop: Xfce live image, or your choice

highlights.light: Lean and fast, with its own runit init system.
highlights.diy: Minimal base you assemble yourself; great for learning.

caveats: Small community; fewer guides.
Mostly manual setup.
Needs Secure Boot turned off to install.

distros.name: Gentoo

highlights.diy: The deepest hands-on Linux: you choose and (optionally) compile everything.
highlights.customizable: Every package can be built with exactly the features you want.

caveats: Install takes hours to days and is fully manual.
Not for a first Linux.
Needs Secure Boot turned off to install.

distros.name: Solus

highlights.beginner: Independent desktop-focused distro with a curated, polished feel.
highlights.stable: Curated rolling release: weekly, tested update batches.

caveats: Small team and a smaller software catalogue (Flatpak fills gaps).
Independent package format, so fewer outside guides apply.

distros.name: AlmaLinux

highlights.enterprise: Binary-compatible with Red Hat Enterprise Linux: matches many workplaces' servers.
highlights.stable: Ten-year support cycle; almost nothing changes under you.
highlights.rhel_family: Same software and commands as Red Hat Enterprise Linux, so work skills and scripts carry straight over.

caveats: Built for servers and workstations, not gaming or the newest hardware.
Desktop software is old; many apps come from EPEL or Flatpak.
